additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by Courts and Tribunals Judiciary
additions.locator: Paras 152-154 (data protection impact assessment); paras 199-201 (public sector equality duty), PDF pp.33 and 42-43
additions.quote: the DPIA failed properly to assess the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
additions.why: The leading UK judgment on a pre-deployment assessment that existed but did not do its job. The force had written an impact assessment for live facial recognition; the court held it inadequate, and held that the force had not done all it reasonably could to check the software for race or sex bias before using it. Shows that a gate is judged on whether it weighed the real risks, not on whether a document exists. A police case under Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018, not the UK GDPR.

additions.title: Equality Act 2010, section 149: Public sector equality duty
additions.quote: A person who is not a public authority but who exercises public functions must, in the exercise of those functions, have due regard
additions.why: A second statutory gate beside the impact assessment: public bodies, and private bodies carrying out public functions, must have due regard to eliminating discrimination and advancing equality when they decide. The Court of Appeal applied it to the decision to deploy an AI system in Bridges. It does not bind a private company acting for itself. The page lists changes from a 2025 Act not yet applied to the Equality Act.

additions.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
additions.locator: List of processing operations requiring a DPIA, item 'Innovative technology'; section 'What does 'innovative technologies' mean?'
additions.quote: processing involving the use of innovative technologies, or the novel application of existing technologies (including AI)
additions.why: Says when the legal gate opens for AI: innovative technology, which the regulator says includes AI, needs an impact assessment when combined with another risk factor from the European list. It is not a rule that every AI use needs one. Under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act; the page carries no date, so the year is the year read.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
additions.locator: Section 'Governance', paragraphs on the AI governance board and the ethics committee
additions.quote: You can include an ethics committee as part of your governance framework, depending on your operating context.
additions.why: Government's own description of an ethics committee for AI: it assesses the ethical implications of projects and decisions, is more specialised than the governance board, and usually includes legal experts and outside representatives. Optional even for departments, and the text gives the committee no power to stop a project. Guidance for the public sector, not law.

additions.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.quote: shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights that the use of such system may produce
additions.why: The nearest thing in law to an ethics gate wider than data protection: before deploying, public bodies, private providers of public services and deployers of the systems in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III (5(b) is credit scoring) must assess the effect on fundamental rights and notify the market surveillance authority of the result. It requires an assessment, not a power to refuse. Paragraphs 4 and 5 are marked as amended by the Digital Omnibus. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. EU law: reaches UK firms only where a system or its output is used in the EU. No application date is stated here.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (US)
additions.locator: Table 4, MANAGE 1.1, p.32 (PDF p.37); Part 1 section on go/no-go decisions
additions.quote: A determination is made as to whether the AI system achieves its intended purposes and stated objectives and whether its development or deployment should proceed.
additions.why: International comparator. Makes the stop-or-go decision an explicit, recorded step, and elsewhere speaks of 'explicit processes for making go/no-go system commissioning and deployment decisions'. Voluntary US framework; it does not say who should hold the decision or call for outside input.

additions.title: How to design an AI ethics board
additions.publisher: Jonas Schuett, Anka Reuel and Alexis Carlier (arXiv preprint 2304.07249)
additions.quote: How should it make decisions and should its decisions be binding?
additions.why: Sets out the five design choices for an ethics board: responsibilities, legal structure, membership, whether its decisions bind, and resources. Useful for reading an answer at the 'power to refuse' level. Conceptual paper drawing on past failures of company ethics boards, aimed at AI developers; preprint as read, no data.

additions.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
additions.publisher: Inioluwa Deborah Raji and others, ACM FAT* 2020 (authors' copy on arXiv)
additions.quote: it remains challenging for practitioners to identify the harmful repercussions of their own systems prior to deployment
additions.why: Proposes an internal audit carried out in stages before release, each stage producing documents that are judged against the organisation's own stated principles. A model for what a review step should receive and record. A proposed framework, not an evaluation of results.

additions.title: Walking the Walk of AI Ethics: Organizational Challenges and the Individualization of Risk among Ethics Entrepreneurs
additions.publisher: Sanna J. Ali and others, ACM FAccT 2023 (authors' copy on arXiv)
additions.quote: they struggle to have ethics prioritized in an environment centered around software product launches
additions.why: Empirical evidence for why informal concern-raising fails: a qualitative study of technology workers responsible for AI ethics found policy, practice and outcome decoupled, ethics losing to launch dates and metrics, and individuals carrying personal risk for raising issues. Supports a defined gate with authority over one that relies on goodwill. Technology companies only; the abstract gives no sample size or country.

additions.title: Algorithmic impact assessment: a case study in healthcare
additions.locator: Section 'Proposed process', step 2 'Application filtering'; Annex 2, Data Access Committee terms of reference
additions.quote: the DAC can choose to either reject NMIP applications at this stage, or invite applicants to proceed to the participatory workshop
additions.why: A worked UK design for a gate with power to refuse: applicants for NHS medical imaging data complete an impact assessment, patients and the public test it in a workshop, and a committee decides whether access is granted. Shows outside input built into the gate. A proposal for an NHS AI Lab trial, not a report of results; independent research institute, not peer reviewed.

additions.title: West Midlands Police Data, Technology and Operational Ethics Panel
additions.publisher: West Midlands Police and Crime Commissioner
additions.locator: Section 'What is the West Midlands Police Data, Technology and Operational Ethics Panel?'
additions.quote: The Panel's job will be to advise the PCC and Chief Constable on data science projects being proposed by WMP's Data Analytics Lab.
additions.why: A standing UK example of external ethics input on proposed data science projects; its reports and minutes are published. Its role as stated is to advise; the decision stays with the Commissioner and Chief Constable. A public body's own description of its committee, undated (year is the year read); one police force, not a general model.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. One addition worth a line in the next version: the brief says the legal gate 'covers data protection only'; for public bodies and private bodies carrying out public functions the public sector equality duty is a second pre-decision duty, and the Court of Appeal enforced both against an AI deployment in Bridges (2020). The UNESCO paragraphs 51 to 53, recorded as unread in the first pass, were read verbatim today and say what the brief says.
